title: Seahawks QB Sam Darnold Out vs. Cardinals: Injury Sidelines Starter for Crucial Pacific Division Clash
body:
Seattle’s quarterback room will be reshuffled once again this week as Sam Darnold was ruled out for Sunday’s matchup with the Arizona Cardinals. The 26‑year‑old veteran suffered a quadriceps strain late in the 27‑20 loss to Chicago, and team doctors confirmed the injury will keep him sidelined for at least the next game. Backup quarterback Drew Locke, who stepped in for Darnold earlier in the season, is expected to take the helm against a Cardinals defense that has struggled to contain opposing passers but remains opportunistic in the secondary.

The injury marks the second time this season the Seahawks have been forced to start a backup quarterback against Arizona, a rivalry that has taken on added significance after Seattle’s disappointing 3‑5 start. Darnold, who was acquired in a trade with the Carolina Panthers last offseason, has been under pressure to justify Seattle’s investment. In his three starts, he posted a 2‑1 record but also threw three interceptions and posted a passer rating just above 80. The quadriceps strain, which appears to be a Grade 2 tear, could linger beyond a single week, raising concerns about the depth chart and the team’s ability to sustain offensive momentum.

Locke, a former fifth‑round pick who spent three seasons on the practice squad before earning a roster spot, brings a different skill set to the field. Known for his mobility and quick decision‑making, he has shown flashes of poise in limited action, completing 61 percent of his passes for 210 yards and a touchdown in his most recent appearance. However, his lack of experience against a disciplined Arizona unit could prove problematic. The Cardinals, led by quarterback Kyler Murray, have averaged 285 passing yards per game and rank fourth in the league in third‑down conversions. Seattle’s offensive line, already tested by injuries to left tackle Charles Cross and guard Ethan Cox, will need to provide Locke with ample protection to avoid a repeat of the Bears’ late‑game collapse.

Head coach Pete Carroll has emphasized that the Seahawks will adapt their game plan to accommodate Locke’s strengths. In press conferences, Carroll noted that the playbook will feature more roll‑outs, screen passes, and short‑zone concepts designed to get the ball out of Locke’s hands quickly and mitigate the pressure from Arizona’s pass rush, anchored by edge rusher J.J. Watt. Defensive coordinator Jim Lombardi (no relation) also hinted at a more aggressive approach on the front side, hoping to generate turnovers that could offset any offensive shortfalls.

The broader implications of Darnold’s absence extend beyond this weekend’s contest. Seattle’s offensive identity has yet to solidify, oscillating between a run‑heavy scheme anchored by running back Kenneth Walker III and a pass‑first approach that leverages Darnold’s arm strength. With the quarterback spot in flux, the Seahawks risk falling further behind in the NFC West race, where the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers have already secured winning records. Moreover, the injury underscores the importance of depth at the most critical position in the NFL, a lesson the Seahawks felt acutely after losing starting left tackle Luke Joe in Week 2.

Looking ahead, the Seahawks will need to manage Darnold’s recovery carefully while giving Locke a chance to prove his viability as a starter. If Locke can orchestrate a win against Arizona, he could earn a larger role in the offense, forcing Carroll to make tough decisions about the quarterback hierarchy moving forward. Conversely, a poor performance could deepen the team’s woes and prompt a reevaluation of the roster before the trade deadline. As the season progresses, Seattle’s ability to adapt to injuries and maximize the talent on its roster will be the decisive factor in determining whether the Seahawks can rebound from a rocky start and reassert themselves as contenders in the Pacific division.
